pharm: Concentrated source of ionized calcium (27 mg or 1.4 mEq elemental calcium per mL of 10% solution) for IV correction of acute symptomatic hypocalcemia; about three times more elemental calcium per volume than calcium gluconate.
quick: 200-1000 mg slow IV; max rate 1 mL/min (100 mg/min)
Acceptable; maternal hypocalcemia itself is harmful
Start at lowest dose; monitor calcium frequently
Serum calcium, ECG, IV site for extravasation
summary: Calcium chloride injection is a concentrated parenteral calcium salt used to treat acute symptomatic hypocalcemia; it is also used in emergencies for hyperkalemia-induced cardiotoxicity, hypermagnesemia, and calcium channel blocker/beta-blocker overdose. It provides about 27 mg (1.4 mEq) elemental calcium per mL of the 10% solution. It must be given slowly IV, preferably through a central or large vein, because extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis. Never give IM or SC.
indications: Emergency treatment of severe hyperkalemia with cardiac toxicity (cardiac membrane stabilization)
Adjunct in calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker overdose
Calcium replacement during massive/citrated blood transfusion (off-label/supportive)

dosage.t: Repeat as needed based on serum calcium
dosage.n: Max infusion rate 1 mL/min (100 mg/min); 10% solution = 100 mg/mL
Stabilizes cardiac membrane; does not lower potassium
Monitor calcium frequently; watch calcium-phosphorus product

admin: Administer by slow IV injection or infusion through a central line or large/deep vein; never IM or SC (causes tissue necrosis and calcinosis cutis)
Do not exceed 1 mL/min (100 mg/min); rapid administration may cause vasodilation, hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, syncope, or cardiac arrest
Warm to body temperature and ensure patency of the vein before injection
Keep the patient recumbent and monitor cardiac status during administration
Stop immediately and treat if extravasation occurs
moa: Intravenous calcium chloride increases serum ionized calcium concentration, restoring normal cellular function (neuromuscular transmission, cardiac and smooth muscle contraction). In hyperkalemia it raises the cardiac cell action-potential threshold, stabilizing the myocardial membrane against arrhythmias.

absolute: Asystole and electromechanical dissociation (pulseless electrical activity)

preg: Not expected to cause birth defects; maternal hypocalcemia itself poses risks (spontaneous abortion, preeclampsia). Use as needed for symptomatic hypocalcemia.
lact: Calcium is present in human milk; administration of the recommended dose is not expected to harm a breastfed infant.
renal: Use cautiously; start at the lowest dose (200 mg) and monitor serum calcium frequently (e.g., every 4 hours). Risk of an elevated calcium-phosphorus product. Aluminum content may accumulate in renal impairment.

major: Digoxin/digitalis glycosides (calcium increases risk of serious arrhythmias and toxicity - avoid concomitant IV use)
moderate: Other calcium-containing or vitamin D products (additive hypercalcemia)
minor: May reduce absorption/effect of certain oral drugs if given enterally (not relevant to IV)
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum calcium and ECG; physically incompatible with many phosphate- and carbonate-containing IV solutions (precipitation).

serious: Extravasation with tissue necrosis, ulceration, and calcinosis cutis

monitoring: Continuous ECG/cardiac monitoring during administration, especially with digoxin
IV site for signs of extravasation
Serum magnesium, phosphate, and potassium as clinically indicated
counsel: This is an emergency/hospital injection given through a vein, preferably a central line
Tell your care team if you feel burning at the IV site - it can damage tissue
You may feel warmth or a chalky taste during the injection - this is expected
Inform your clinician if you take digoxin (heart medicine) or have kidney problems
Cardiac monitoring will be performed during the injection
pk: Transient; depends on dose and ongoing losses
20-25 C (68-77 F); do not use if cloudy or containing precipitate
pearls: 10% calcium chloride provides ~27 mg (1.4 mEq) elemental calcium per mL - about 3x more than the same volume of 10% calcium gluconate
Preferred over calcium gluconate in emergencies (e.g., cardiac arrest, severe hyperkalemia) because it delivers calcium faster
Strongly prefer a central line; extravasation causes severe necrosis - never give IM or SC
Do NOT mix with bicarbonate, phosphate, or ceftriaxone (precipitation)
In hyperkalemia it protects the heart but does not lower serum potassium
missed: Given acutely by clinicians titrated to serum calcium and clinical response; no scheduled missed-dose concept. Redose based on repeat calcium levels.
overdose: Overdose causes hypercalcemia: shortened QT interval, bradycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting, lethargy, seizures, and coma. Discontinue immediately, provide IV fluids and supportive care; consider loop diuretics, calcitonin, or other measures to lower calcium. Monitor ECG and calcium.
